card.hook: Angkor Wat is the world's largest religious complex, and it doesn't hide it: a wide moat, an outer wall, then three galleries stepping up to five towers. Even a quick snap from here comes out looking tidy and grand.
card.stand_here: Stand about 160 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. The middle of the temple is about 2 minutes on foot from there.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the galleries, towers and moat. Use 1x for most views, since it looks the most natural. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tower tops and carvings on the walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the towers or galleries with a horizontal line so the temple doesn't lean, and leave some stonework or open ground in front to show how big it is.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can be harsh on the pale stone and make the shadows dark.
card.selfie_here: Head to the North and South Libraries near the entrance and stand in front of one of the library doorways. Use your front camera and turn so the temple towers sit far behind you over your shoulder. It's a nicely framed selfie without the crowds at the reflecting pools.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the front-left corner of the north (left) reflecting pool, with the full temple and its reflection behind you, and ask a passer-by to shoot back towards you.
card.rules_and_safety: Angkor Wat is an active place of Buddhist worship, so check the official site before you go for current visiting rules. The upper gallery is reached by steep stairs, so use the handrails.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole temple, then walk closer and find a carved figure (a devata) that looks like it's smiling at you.
card.good_to_know: Angkor Wat was built in the 12th century for the Khmer king Suryavarman II, first as a Hindu temple to Vishnu. Over the centuries it became a Buddhist temple, and people still worship there today. Unlike most temples around Angkor, it faces west.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 160 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. The middle of the temple is about 2 minutes on foot from there.

card.hook: Walk in among the Bayon's towers and you'll feel watched, in the friendliest way. Smiling stone faces look out from every side, so you can find a new angle every few steps.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the base of one of the central face towers, where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the tower, tilt your phone up and let the huge face fill the frame.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x right at the base to make the face look enormous and the lines lean in. Step back and switch to 1x to get whole towers against the sky. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for single faces and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the face, then slide the brightness down a touch so the bright sky doesn't wash out the stone, and switch on gridlines to see how the lines lean in.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the low sun brings out the carving. Warm late sun is lovely if you can line up three towers in one frame.
card.selfie_here: Guides recommend the northeast corner of the upper terrace, where one face looks straight at you while another shows in profile behind it. Use the front camera at 0.5x, with the towers over your shoulder. The upper terrace has been reported closed for restoration, so check what's open when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the open lawn in front of the temple, slightly to the right of the main walkway so the towers rise behind you, and ask a passer-by to shoot from the walkway side.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are banned across Angkor without a special permit, and posted photo rules and staff guidance can change by zone. The stairs are steep and worn, so wear good shoes.
card.challenge: Find a face that seems to be smiling right at you, then see if you can catch a second face peeking in behind it.
card.good_to_know: The Bayon has 216 carved faces, which many scholars read as portraits of King Jayavarman VII. He built it in the late 12th or early 13th century at the centre of his walled capital, Angkor Thom. It was the last state temple built at Angkor, and it's still a Buddhist sanctuary, so check the official site for tickets, opening times and dress expectations.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole arch and the lit street into one frame. Zoom 1x looks more natural and usually copes better in the dark, while 2x or 5x can pick out the arch lights but often struggles at night.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the arch, then slide the brightness down a touch so the neon stays rich instead of turning white.
card.best_time: Go after dark, once the neon is on. A wet night is even better, so if it rains, wait for the shower to ease and shoot while the ground is still shiny.

card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally fine in public areas of Pub Street, but ask permission before taking close-ups of individual people. Crime is described as very low, but keep an eye on your valuables, including your phone.

card.hook: Picture a stone tug-of-war that's been going on for centuries: gods pulling on the left, demons on the right, and a giant calm face watching from above like the referee. That's the road into Angkor Thom.
card.stand_here: Stand on the causeway in front of Tonle Om Gate, on either side of the bridge over the moat. The gate is about 1.7 km north of the Angkor Wat entrance. Face the gate tower so the rows of statues lead straight to it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the moat, causeway, statues and gate tower all in one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer view of the gate, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the carved faces.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the causeway in the middle so the rows of statues lead your eye to the gate.
card.best_time: Come early in the morning or late in the afternoon. The light is softer and there are fewer tuk-tuks and tour groups in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Leave the parking area and walk to the moat edge on the side where the local wooden boats are moored. It's quieter and further from the traffic. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt it so the gate and walls sit over your shoulder across the water. Check the angle on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at ground level on the southern approach of the causeway and shoot back toward the gate, while you stand on the stone road so the face tower rises above you (and stay clear of the vehicle lane).
card.rules_and_safety: Vehicles use the causeway and this is still a road entrance, so keep an eye out for traffic while you line up your shot. You need an Angkor pass for the park, so check the official site for current rules before you go.
card.challenge: Get the gods on the left, the demons on the right and the giant face on top, all in one picture. Then count how many tuk-tuks sneak in anyway.
card.good_to_know: Angkor Thom means 'Great City'. It was the last and longest-lasting capital of the Khmer Empire, founded in the late twelfth century by King Jayavarman VII. Its walls are 8 m high and 3 km long on each side, with a moat around them. The tug-of-war on the causeway shows the Churning of the Sea of Milk myth, and the gate tower is about 23 m high.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the causeway in front of Tonle Om Gate, on either side of the bridge over the moat. The gate is about 1.7 km north of the Angkor Wat entrance. Face the gate tower so the rows of statues lead straight to it.

card.hook: Picture tree roots pouring over the corner of a stone gate like frozen syrup, with a temple tower peeking out behind them. One photographer's guide calls this the most photographed spung tree in Ta Prohm, and you're about to see why.
card.stand_here: Stand at the northwest corner of the East Gate, the entry tower of the fourth enclosure, where the phone icon is. Face the corner so the roots are in front of you and the tower rises behind them. If you can, stand a little above the timber posing platform so it stays out of the shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the roots and the gate tower together. If you're close, try zoom 0.5x to fit the whole root mass and the tower in. Zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) is handy for root details, or for cropping out the platform and other visitors.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines to keep the tower upright, then tap the roots and nudge the picture darker if the sky behind the tower looks washed out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when few people are around, according to a photographer's guide to the temple. You'll have a better chance of a frame with no platform and no strangers in it.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden platform beside the wall by the tree roots in the northwest courtyard. A guide page names it as a selfie spot, and it's quieter than the famous Tomb Raider tree. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the roots fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the wooden bridge over the first moat, on the trail in from the West gate, hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to shoot you on the old stone causeway.
card.rules_and_safety: Ta Prohm is inside Angkor Archaeological Park, so you need an Angkor pass. Check the official site for current rules and opening times, and stay on the marked wooden paths. The famous Tomb Raider doorway may be roped off, so check when you arrive. Bugs and spiders live in the moist hollow of the tree near the start of the route, so check before you sit in it for a photo.
card.challenge: Get the roots big in the foreground and the tower perfectly straight behind them, with no stranger in the frame. Gridlines make it easier than it sounds.
card.good_to_know: King Jayavarman VII founded Ta Prohm in 1186 as a monastery dedicated to his mother. The stones were laid without mortar, so once the place was abandoned, trees took root in the loosened stonework. Conservation work in the 20th century deliberately left much of it looking as it was found, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the northwest corner of the East Gate, the entry tower of the fourth enclosure, where the phone icon is. Face the corner so the roots are in front of you and the tower rises behind them. If you can, stand a little above the timber posing platform so it stays out of the shot.

card.hook: Picture a stone doorway with a giant tree hugging the wall beside it, and fallen blocks lying where they dropped. That's Preah Khan, and it's left mostly as it was found, so you get texture everywhere you point your phone.
card.stand_here: Head to the east gate, the traditional main entrance, and stand back from it. Face the doorway so it frames a single carved yoni (a stone base) in the foreground, with a line of repeating doorways behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the doorway frames the scene naturally. Switch to 0.5x for the long causeway or tight passages, and try 2x or more (depending on your phone) for carvings and those repeating doorways.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the yoni low in the frame and keep your phone level so the stone arches don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. Check the official site for opening times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the causeway just past the east gate. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the garuda carvings on the enclosure wall behind you, and pick the garudas further along the wall, because the first one by the gate is worn and hard to make out. On your way out, turn back on the exit causeway for a shot with the temple's moat reflection behind you.
card.ask_someone: On the path up to the east gate, stand beside the lions with the gate in view and ask the passer-by to stand back on the approach, so the gate fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't climb on the structures or touch the carvings, and ask permission before photographing locals or monks. Follow any posted guidance about restricted areas. Stone can get slippery, especially in rain and storms, so watch your footing.
card.challenge: Find a spot where a tree and a doorway share the frame, then see if you can line up the doorways so your eye runs straight through the temple.
card.good_to_know: Preah Khan means "Royal Sword". King Jayavarman VII built it in the 12th century as a Buddhist temple in honour of his father. It once worked as a city, a temple and a Buddhist university all in one. The outer wall measures about 800 by 700 m, so allow time to wander.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the east gate, the traditional main entrance, and stand back from it. Face the doorway so it frames a single carved yoni (a stone base) in the foreground, with a line of repeating doorways behind it.

card.hook: Picture a red-brick pyramid glowing like a hot coal while the sun sinks toward the Angkor Wat towers. That's Pre Rup in late light, and you get to climb it.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on Pre Rup, on the west edge of the upper terrace. Face west, out over the rice fields.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the wide view across the rice fields. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the faraway Angkor Wat towers closer. From ground level, zoom 0.5x helps fit all five towers in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the sky near the sun and slide it a little darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset, the last hour or two of daylight, is the sweet spot. Get there early enough to claim a spot on the terrace before the light turns. Sunrise works too, when the eastern face and central tower catch the first light.
card.selfie_here: Try the main stairs on the north, south or west sides, not the east, and snap yourself climbing with the front camera. For a calmer shot, use the upper terrace on the side away from the sunset crowd, with the temple towers over your shoulder at 0.5x.
card.ask_someone: For a full-temple shot of you, head to the road on the east side (walk round from the south side), where the temple is seen from the road, and ask a passer-by to snap you there.
card.rules_and_safety: The steps are steep and have no railings, so take your time and keep a hand free. Pre Rup is inside the Angkor Archaeological Park, which needs an Angkor pass, and opening hours vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Count the five towers (one at each corner, one in the middle), then get all five in a single frame from ground level.
card.good_to_know: Pre Rup was built as the state temple of the Khmer king Rajendravarman and dedicated in 961 or early 962. It rises in three steep tiers of brick, laterite and sandstone. The name means 'turn the body', from a popular belief that funerals were once held here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on Pre Rup, on the west edge of the upper terrace. Face west, out over the rice fields.

card.hook: Most people climb Phnom Bakheng to watch Angkor Wat shrink into the jungle. You can be a bit sneakier: turn around and photograph the temple you're standing on, with the last sun glowing on the stone.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the northern terrace of the upper tiers of Phnom Bakheng. Face the carved panels and sanctuary walls, where the low sun hits them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for carvings and stonework. Try 2x or 5x to pick out a single detail. From the summit, 5x or higher (depending on your phone) brings in Angkor Wat's towers, about 1.5 km to the southeast, but expect them to look small.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line up a carved panel or sanctuary wall along one line, keep some terrace stone in the foreground for depth, and tap the stonework so it's sharp.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, when the low sun lights up the carvings. Get in place well before sunset, because one guide says the sunset lookout can fill by 5 pm. Head down soon after the sun goes.
card.selfie_here: Try the northern terrace, which is less crowded than the summit, and use the front camera with the carved temple behind you. For an Angkor Wat selfie, the wooden lookout on the upper level, at the southern edge of the eastern side, should put the towers in your background. Check both spots on the ground, and try 0.5x to fit more in.
card.rules_and_safety: The climb is steep and the steps near the top are very narrow, so take your time. Selfie sticks are reported banned in the Angkor temple zones (from a secondary blog), while handheld phones are fine. You need an Angkor pass, and summit numbers are limited, so check the official site before you go. There's no lighting after closing.
card.challenge: Catch the last sunlight sliding across one carved panel, then sneak a sanctuary into the corner of your next shot.
card.good_to_know: Phnom Bakheng was built at the end of the 9th century, in the reign of King Yasovarman (889–910). It rises about 65 m above the plain as a seven-level pyramid, with five sandstone sanctuaries on the top level. Most of the 108 small towers that once surrounded it have collapsed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the northern terrace of the upper tiers of Phnom Bakheng. Face the carved panels and sanctuary walls, where the low sun hits them.

card.hook: Picture colourful water lilies, a few lazy fish and the odd turtle, with a pagoda roof rising over the water. That's the quiet side of Wat Damnak, and it's a lot more peaceful than the usual temple shot.
card.stand_here: Walk into the grounds and follow the paths to the lily pond. The phone icon on the map is right at the subject, so stand at the water's edge and face the pond, with the pagoda and trees behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the pond, the lilies and the pagoda in one frame. Drop to 0.5x to get low and close to the lilies. Try 2x or more (it depends on your phone) for the pagoda roof or a single flower, so you don't have to lean over the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the water's edge on the lower line and the pagoda roof on an upper third, then tap a lily and slide darker a touch so the white petals keep their detail.
card.best_time: Try to avoid school hours, since this is a working monastery school. Light on the water is usually softest early or late in the day.
card.selfie_here: Head for the lily pond beside the long, narrow water feature along the front of the library building, where the waterlilies are varied. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the lilies fill the space behind you.
card.ask_someone: Halfway across the stone bridge at the south-east corner of Old Market (Phsar Chas), the pagoda roof sits to your slight right, so ask someone to shoot you there (just the roof shows, not the whole pagoda).
card.rules_and_safety: Dress accordingly, don't wear a hat, and take your shoes off if you go inside. Keep your voice down, stay on the paths, and ask before photographing monks or pupils.
card.challenge: Can you get a lily, a fish and the pagoda roof all in one frame? Extra points if a turtle photobombs.
card.good_to_know: King Sisowath lived here from 1904 to 1927, which is why the name recalls a royal home. After the palace moved, the old courtyard became a pagoda. In the 1950s the monks added stupas in the courtyard, modelled on Banteay Srei, and the Center for Khmer Studies is in the grounds too.

card.hook: This building is big. Really big. Stand too close to the doors and you'll get a lovely picture of... a door. Back up and let the whole front of the Angkor National Museum fit on your screen.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, which marks the museum itself. Then step back from the entrance until the whole front fits your screen, rather than shooting from right beside the doors.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x from a little way back to fit the whole building in. Switch to 1x for a natural view of the entrance, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details or signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, hold your phone upright and level, and line up the building's flat edges with them so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the front of the building than midday. If the sky is very bright, tap the building on screen and slide it a bit darker so the walls keep their detail.
card.selfie_here: Head to the outdoor terrace in the museum grounds, a replica of the Terrace of the Leper King from Angkor Thom. It makes a different backdrop, and one page suggests golden hour for warm light. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more in, and keep the terrace behind you. The Garden of the Gods, with its replica temple statues, is a second option with soft daytime light.
card.ask_someone: In the entrance courtyard, hand your phone to a friendly passer-by, stand near the entrance, and ask them to step back until the whole front fits in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are not allowed. Photo rules inside can differ from room to room, and sources disagree on what's allowed, so look for signs and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get one shot of the whole building with a few visitors walking in, so everyone can see just how big it really is.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened on 12 November 2007. Its eight galleries tell the story of the Khmer Empire's Angkor period, roughly the 9th to 14th centuries. Themes include the Gallery of 1,000 Buddha, the great Khmer kings, Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom, and apsara dancers. Wipe your lens before you start, because humid air and fingerprints can soften pictures.

card.hook: Most people crowd round the five-headed horse at the northern platform, but the Leper King end of this wall is much quieter. Its weathered, sunken carvings are made for slow, close-up photos.
card.stand_here: Stand at the north end of the Terrace of the Elephants, where it meets the Terrace of the Leper King, and face the carvings. The long elephant wall runs away to the south, and the middle of the terrace is about 3 minutes on foot that way.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the sculptures on the Leper King terrace. Tap 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for worn faces and carved lines, and try 0.5x only if you step back to show the length of the wall.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the carving, then slide the brightness down a touch so the stone keeps its texture and the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Check the light on the day, but going earlier or later than midday usually helps the carvings. Late afternoon can get busy with wedding photo shoots on the Royal Square.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the grass strip right below the wall, facing the carved elephant panels, so they sit behind you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if you want more wall in the shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the road from the terrace while you stand in front of the wall. A guide says that side gives a sweeping view of the whole wall, which is roughly 350 m long.
card.rules_and_safety: Carry water, because vendors may not be around when you need them most and the heat can be intense. This is part of the Angkor Thom complex, so entry may be ticketed or restricted. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one close shot of a single worn face, then step back and take one that shows where it sits on the wall.
card.good_to_know: King Jayavarman VII used this wall as a platform to watch his army return in triumph. It was also the base for his grand audience hall. The wall is about 350 metres long, and it's named for the elephants carved on its eastern face.

card.hook: Picture a long, low stone wall resting quietly on the far side of a big sheet of water while the morning sky wakes up. That's Banteay Kdei from the Srah Srang terrace, and it's a calmer start than the Angkor Wat crowds.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Srah Srang terrace, at the east edge of the basin, and face west across the water. The temple's east gate is roughly 500 m away, with its long sandstone wall stretching along beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the water, gate and wall all fit in. Then try zoom 2x up to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the gate and the line of the wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the lower line so the water fills the foreground, then tap the gate and drag the slider down a touch to make it darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning, around sunrise. The light changes fast, so take a few shots. It's usually less busy than Angkor Wat at that hour, but crowds are never guaranteed.
card.selfie_here: Try the sandstone landing terrace with the naga balustrades at Srah Srang. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to fit in more, and check the preview to see what's over your shoulder before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the stone landing stage and shoot back across the road, while you stand in front of the temple's east entrance gate.
card.rules_and_safety: Expect uneven stone, steps and narrow passages in places inside the temple. Some towers and corridors are roped off, so your view may be partly blocked. If someone offers to guide you or show you photo spots, agree a price first or politely say no.
card.challenge: Get the whole scene in one shot with the water filling the bottom and the gate sitting neatly along the top line. Bonus points if nobody's thumb sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: Banteay Kdei is a Buddhist temple from the mid-12th to early 13th century, built under Jayavarman VII in the Bayon style. It's like Ta Prohm and Preah Khan, but smaller and simpler. The east gate is cross-shaped with carved faces of Lokesvara. Monks lived here on and off until the 1960s, and restoration work is still going on.

card.hook: The big reclining Buddha on the Baphuon is a sneaky one: there's no statue to spot, just an outline hiding in the stonework. Once your eye catches it, you can't unsee it.
card.stand_here: Walk to the open ground on the west side of the Baphuon, right where the phone icon sits, and turn to face the temple. Stand well back so the whole wall is in view, because that's where the Buddha's outline shows up.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the whole western wall in the frame, then go to 1x for a natural look. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the carved outline and the stone texture.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, keep them level with the stepped tiers, and place the Buddha's outline along one line. Then tap the stone wall and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out the carving.
card.best_time: Afternoon is suggested for the western side, but check how the light looks on the day. Upper areas can close in the late afternoon, so don't leave your climb too late.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the reclining Buddha on the western face of the temple, which a guide says photographs best in the afternoon. Use the front camera at 0.5x, stand with your back to the wall and let the big stone tiers sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back on the raised causeway on the eastern approach, while you stand further along it facing them, so the pyramid rises behind you as far as it fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear comfortable shoes, as there are many steep steps and uneven stone paths. You need an Angkor Archaeological Park pass, so check the official site for current access rules and any limits on the upper terrace. One blogger also asks people to put away selfie sticks in crowds, since they knock into people.
card.challenge: Play detective: find the Buddha's outline without looking at a guide, then get a shot where a friend points at it from the right spot.
card.good_to_know: The Baphuon was built in the mid-11th century as the state temple of Suryavarman I, first for Shiva and later as a Buddhist temple. The reclining Buddha is about 9 metres tall and 70 metres long, and recent carbon dating puts it in the 15th century. When work stopped in 1970 the collapsed stones were left in numbered blocks, and the temple finally reopened in 2011.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the open ground on the west side of the Baphuon, right where the phone icon sits, and turn to face the temple. Stand well back so the whole wall is in view, because that's where the Buddha's outline shows up.

card.hook: Picture a tiny stone temple sitting on a round island in the middle of a pool, with carved snake tails curling around its base like they're guarding it. That's Neak Pean, and the curves look great against the water.
card.stand_here: Walk the long wooden causeway to the circular platform around the island at Neak Pean, right where the phone icon is. Face the central tower.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the island and tower together. Go to 0.5x on the causeway to fit in the water and bare trees, then 2x to 5x for the carved snake tails and the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the tower upright, then tap the tower and slide the picture a little darker if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light and fewer people. The wet season fills the pool for good reflections, while the dry season can leave it empty and muddy.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the long wooden boardwalk, which guides call the most photogenic part of the site, with water and lotus around it. Use the front camera at 0.5x and try to get the island shrine over your shoulder. Check the framing on the spot to see how much of the island fits behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the southern end of the boardwalk facing north toward the island shrine, while you pose out on the boardwalk in front of it, ideally in morning light with the sun behind them.
card.rules_and_safety: You can't go onto the central island, and you shouldn't climb or touch the temple. One visitor says the wooden walkway has no handrails and sits just above the water, so watch your step while you line up the shot. You need an Angkor Pass to get in.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the curved snake tails sit along the bottom third of your frame, with the tower standing straight above them. Snake-and-tower, nailed.
card.good_to_know: Neak Pean means "the entwined serpents", after the carved nagas around the island's base. It was built in the reign of King Jayavarman VII and is linked to Preah Khan. Four small pools around the central one stand for water, earth, fire and wind, and the horse statue Balaha is the only original sculpture still standing in the water.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk the long wooden causeway to the circular platform around the island at Neak Pean, right where the phone icon is. Face the central tower.

card.hook: Before you dive into the busy aisles, here's a calmer way to meet Old Market: the whole roofed building sits across the river, with the water laid out in front like a welcome mat.
card.stand_here: Stand on Old Market Bridge, on the east bank approach, and face west across the Siem Reap River to the market.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the main river-and-market view. Switch to 0.5x if the roofline gets cut off or you want more water, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for market details across the river.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the water along the lower third and the roofline across the middle, and keep your phone level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water, while the market is livelier during the day. Take a quick shot at each end of the day and see which one you like.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try 0.5x, and turn so the market roofline sits over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher and check the building isn't sliced off before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside, the aisles are narrow and crowded, so keep your phone close and ask before photographing vendors up close. Conditions may have changed, so check on the day.
card.challenge: Get the water exactly on the lower gridline and the roofline dead level, with bonus points if the building doesn't lean one bit.
card.good_to_know: Old Market is called Phsar Chas in Khmer, and it's in the south of Siem Reap. Locals and visitors both use it, and it's such a fixture that many businesses give their address in relation to it. Stalls sell silk, silverware, T-shirts and wood and stone carvings, and the food area has rice, dried fish, pork sausages, fruit, vegetables and baguettes.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Old Market Bridge, on the east bank approach, and face west across the Siem Reap River to the market.

A local photo-walk or a view from the river side of the market may work, but I could not verify either from a source.

card.hook: Most Angkor temples show off with carvings, but Ta Keo just stands there, big, plain and sandy-gold, and somehow looks better for it. All those clean lines and strong shadows make for a great phone photo.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the temple grounds, and face the pyramid. From here it rises above the jungle canopy, and the trees make a natural frame around the stone.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the pyramid and the trees in one shot. Drop to 0.5x from low on the ground to get the full height, or try 2x to pick out the tops of the towers (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the pyramid on an upper line with a band of treetops below it, then tap the sunlit stone and slide the brightness down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is the sweet spot, when the low light brings out the texture in the sandstone. Morning is good too, and the temple is shaded after about 1 pm, so skip the harsh midday glare.
card.selfie_here: Try the east causeway, the long path running out from the temple's eastern entrance. Use your front camera, hold it a bit low and turn so the temple sits behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand at the southwest corner of the pyramid and frame it with the jungle canopy behind you while you pose.
card.rules_and_safety: Follow any posted signs, respect barriers and closed areas, and ask before photographing worshippers. Photos are generally fine, but some areas under restoration may be off-limits, and drones are restricted. The four stairways are very steep and can be slippery in the rainy season, so take your time.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the five towers poke out above the treetops and get the whole pyramid on your upper gridline, with zero wonky sides.
card.good_to_know: Ta Keo was the state temple of Jayavarman V, who began it in 975, and it was dedicated around 1000. It was never finished, because work stopped just as the carving was starting. That's why it's so plain: five sanctuary towers on a five-tier pyramid, with the summit 21.5 m above the ground.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the temple grounds, and face the pyramid. From here it rises above the jungle canopy, and the trees make a natural frame around the stone.

card.hook: Picture two stone lions at the top of a staircase that runs straight down into a mirror. That's Srah Srang on a still morning, and it's a lot easier to photograph than it looks.
card.stand_here: Stand on the west edge of Srah Srang, at the top of the stone steps down to the jetty, and face east over the water. The terrace is directly across the road from the Banteay Kdei entrance, so you can't miss it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the terrace, the water and the sky all in one shot. Tap 0.5x if you want more of the carved steps and railings in front of you. In the dry season, zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) can pick out the sun over the far trees or the little island stupa.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky, then slide it a little darker so the sunrise colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Sunrise is the star here, when the sun comes up over the trees on the far bank. Get there before dawn, because the terrace can get busy in peak season and you'll want room to choose your spot. Sunset is a good backup, with the sun dropping between the trees.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera on the western landing terrace and stand with the water behind you, so the carved nāga railings, lions and steps fill the foreground. Want it quieter? Try the east end of the lake, on the bank nearest Pre Rup, away from the Banteay Kdei side.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the short path from the road near Banteay Kdei, where the reservoir and the terrace come into view, while you stand with the whole reservoir behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You need an Angkor Pass to enter the Angkor area, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Switch on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line, and keep one lion or nāga railing along the edge. Then wait for the ripples to settle before you press the button. Patience gets you the mirror.
card.good_to_know: Srah Srang means "Royal Bath". It's a reservoir (a baray) dug in the mid-10th century, and it's still partly flooded today. Around the year 1200, Jayavarman VII added the cross-shaped stone landing terrace, where each nāga railing ends in an upright head with a garuda above it.

card.hook: Picture a temple on an island in the middle of a huge lake. Now take away the lake. That's East Mebon today: a stepped stone pyramid standing over a dry plain, guarded by elephants about two metres high.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map marks the middle of the temple. From there, walk to the southwest corner of the lower tier and stand at the foot of the elephant. Face the elephant so the stepped base rises behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and keep a little distance so the whole elephant fits. Then step closer, or use 2x-5x (depending on your phone), for a detail shot of the carving. Use 0.5x for the full temple front or the view from the upper level.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the elephant on one of the vertical lines, then tap the elephant and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its texture.
card.best_time: Sunrise and late afternoon are best, when low light brings out the texture of the stone. For the temple front, go when the morning sun reaches the stonework.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the southwest-corner elephant with the temple behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x to squeeze more of the temple in. For a second option, pose by one of the two lions flanking the staircase to the upper platform, and pick the side where the lions are in better shape.
card.rules_and_safety: You need an Angkor Archaeological Park pass, so check the official site before you go. Ask permission before taking pictures of people. Don't climb on or touch the statues or carvings, or sit or lean on fragile structures, and take care on the steep steps.
card.challenge: Get the elephant sitting neatly on a gridline with the steps rising behind it, then sneak in a close-up of its carving and see which one you like more.
card.good_to_know: East Mebon is a 10th-century temple that once stood on an artificial island in the middle of a huge reservoir, the East Baray. It was dedicated in 953 CE to the Hindu god Shiva and honours the parents of King Rajendravarman. The four landing stages at the base are a reminder that visitors once arrived by boat.
